newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Gold revaluation cannot aid EU budgets - Maystadt.
newsitem.headline: Gold revaluation cannot aid EU budgets - Maystadt.

text.p: Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt said on Thursday he did not believe that a revaluation of gold reserves by European central banks could lower national budget deficits or debt.

Commenting on Germany's proposal to revalue the Bundesbank's gold reserves with market prices, Maystadt told reporters: "I don't see how it's possible to translate the revaluation to a reduction in public deficits."

He cautioned, however, that a favourable decision by Eurostat, the EU's statisical office, on the proposal by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel was a possibility, and if approved would have to apply to all EU countries.
"If (Germany) can find a way, it should be possible for other countries," he said.

Bonn's controversial strategy comes amid a substantial shortfall in the government's revenue projections for 1997, the critical year in which countries will be judged on whether they qualify for a single currency.
Analysts say the Bundesbank is one of the few European central banks that does not revalue its gold and currency reserves on a regular basis.

Maystadt was careful to distinguish between central bank gold sales and revaluation, the former having been used by the Belgian central bank last year to reduce the government's high level of outstanding debt.
Earlier this year, Eurostat ruled that such sales could be used by national governments in lowering their debt levels, but not their deficits.

Separately, when asked whether he favoured an early announcement of how the EU would fix national currencies against the euro, Maystadt said he agreed with the view of Alexandre Lamfalussy, president of the European Monetary Institute, that such a strategy was desirable.
He added that the announcement of a method to lock exchange rates should be made early next year at the time of the decision on which countries qualify for the single currency.

EU governments anxiously want to prevent market speculation from derailing the euro during the period after the decision on which countries will participate, expected in early May 1998, and the launch date, January 1, 1999.
Maystadt said several options for fixing the conversion rates were under consideration, including an average of historical rates.
But he declined to offer a view on which was the best approach. "I don't have a preference for how it is done," he said.

Asked specifically about Luxembourg's proposal that EU governments should announce "indicative" exchange rates for national currencies against the euro later this year, Maystadt said: "There is a risk it could prejudice the judgment of EMU members."
